title: Tokyo’s runway into Central Asia
gist: Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are building out airports and fleets to become Eurasian aviation hubs, and Japan is converting decades of JICA aid into commercial equity — Sojitz holds 30% of the ~US$1bn new Tashkent airport consortium. The authors frame Japanese aviation infrastructure investment as a low-cost geopolitical wedge into a region dominated by China and Russia, tied to Tokyo's US$19bn five-year business-project target and critical-minerals access.

insights.claim: The new major airport in Tashkent is being built by a consortium in which Saudi Arabia's Vision Invest holds 45%, Japan's Sojitz Corporation 30%, South Korea's Incheon International Airport Corporation 15% and Uzbekistan Airports 10%.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Concrete cap-table for a flagship Central Asian infrastructure asset — names the listed and sovereign-linked players with exposure to Uzbek aviation buildout.
insights.locator: The selected companies for this project form a consortium

insights.claim: Sojitz's investment in the Tashkent airport project will reportedly reach around US$1 billion, making commercial aviation a materially new sector for Japanese capital in Central Asia rather than an aid extension.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: A billion-dollar single-project commitment sets a precedent for Japanese trading houses taking equity infrastructure risk in Central Asia.
insights.locator: Sojitz's investment will reportedly reach around US$1 billion

insights.claim: If the new Tashkent airport project goes well, Japanese companies could be invited into further regional aviation projects including modernising Uzbekistan's Bukhara airport, a new passenger terminal in Namangan, and a new airport in Astana.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: A visible pipeline of follow-on tenders — execution on Tashkent is the gating event for a multi-project Japanese franchise.
insights.locator: If the new Tashkent airport project goes well

insights.claim: Japan's JICA already modernised airports in the Uzbek cities of Samarkand, Urgench and Bukhara and reconstructed the airport in Astana, giving Japanese firms an incumbency advantage that commercial deals now monetise.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Aid-funded engagement is converting into commercial mandates — the classic Japanese ODA-to-equity pathway is the template to watch across the region.
insights.locator: Japan has long been a major donor of official development assistance

insights.claim: Kazakh airlines carried 15 million passengers in 2025 while the country's airports served 32 million passengers and handled 173,000 tonnes of cargo.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Baseline traffic figures to size the addressable market for terminal capacity, ground handling and fleet orders in Kazakhstan.
insights.locator: Kazakh airlines carried 15 million passengers in 2025

insights.claim: Kazakhstan recently ordered 25 Airbus A320 aircraft for its airlines, signalling a fleet-led push to expand routes and attract passengers.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Narrowbody demand from Central Asian carriers is a real order-book contributor for Airbus and a driver of MRO and airport-capacity spend.
insights.locator: Kazakhstan recently ordered 25 Airbus A320 aircraft

insights.claim: Kazakhstan aims to establish direct Astana–Tokyo flights by the end of the year, with Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov declaring that international routes "must be opened faster and with competitive ticket prices".
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: A dated, checkable milestone: launch of Astana–Tokyo service would confirm the Japan-Central Asia connectivity thesis is moving from rhetoric to schedule.
insights.quote: must be opened faster and with competitive ticket prices
insights.locator: Kazakhstan aims to establish direct flights between Astana and Tokyo

insights.claim: Russia's war on Ukraine has long disrupted air traffic routes while more recent conflict between Iran and the United States and Israel caused widespread havoc in commercial aviation, making Central Asian corridors valuable as conflict-bypass options.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Airspace closures create structural demand for alternative Eurasian routings — a durable tailwind for Central Asian hub economics independent of tourism.
insights.locator: Russia's war on Ukraine has long disrupted air traffic routes

themes.theme: Tourism flows as the demand story

insights.claim: More than 30,000 Japanese tourists visited Uzbekistan in 2025, an increase of over 40% year on year, per Uzbekistan's National Statistics Committee.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Fast growth off a small base — the volume is still too thin to justify hub economics alone, so the investment case rests on geopolitics plus transit traffic.
insights.locator: According to Uzbekistan's National Statistics Committee

insights.claim: Japanese citizens can travel visa-free to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan while Kazakh and Uzbek nationals still require visas for Japan, an asymmetry that biases flows toward inbound Japanese tourism rather than two-way traffic.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: One-way visa liberalisation caps route load factors; watch for Japanese visa reciprocity as the unlock for sustainable direct service.
insights.locator: Japanese citizens can travel to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan visa-free

insights.claim: Kazakhstan draws lower tourism volumes from Japan than Uzbekistan does, so its hub ambitions depend more on adding frequencies through Astana and Almaty than on existing Japanese leisure demand.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Kazakh airport capex carries higher demand risk than Uzbek capex — differentiate the two markets rather than treating Central Asia as one trade.
insights.locator: Like Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan aims to become a Eurasian hub

themes.theme: Japan's Central Asia strategy and minerals

insights.claim: A joint statement from the 2025 Japan-Central Asia Summit set Japan's goal at around US$19 billion in business projects within the next five years.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: A headline capital target that frames deal-flow expectations for Japanese trading houses and contractors in the region through 2030.
insights.locator: As part of the 2025 Japan-Central Asia Summit

insights.claim: Mining is Tokyo's stated priority in Central Asia given the global contest over critical minerals and rare earth elements, with INPEX, Marubeni, Sumitomo and Mitsui already present in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Aviation infrastructure is the enabler for a minerals play — Japanese trading houses are the listed vehicles for Central Asian critical-minerals exposure.
insights.locator: Mining is a priority for Tokyo

insights.claim: Japan's investment and engagement across Central Asia still pale in comparison to those of China, Russia, Europe and the United States, making aviation a niche where Tokyo can compete rather than a broad challenge to incumbents.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Sizes the ambition realistically — do not overextrapolate Japanese influence in Central Asia from headline summit numbers.
insights.locator: While Japan's investment and engagement across Central Asia pale

insights.claim: Commercial aviation is a relatively new sector for Japanese engagement in Central Asia and could put Japanese and Central Asian business interests on a more equal footing than the donor-recipient dynamic of official development assistance.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Shift from aid to equity changes the risk-return profile: Japanese capital now takes commercial downside, so project selection discipline matters.
insights.locator: Commercial aviation, however, is still a relatively new sector

insights.claim: At the First Central Asia-Japan Dialogue Summit in Tokyo in December 2025, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for expanded tourism and business cooperation, framing person-to-person ties as the political rationale for connectivity spending.
insights.speaker: Wilder Alejandro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Top-level political sponsorship reduces regulatory and route-approval risk for Japan-Central Asia aviation projects.
insights.locator: During the First Central Asia-Japan Dialogue Summit
